title: Unity guide pilot
introduction: Bahá’u’lláh asks why God created everyone from the same dust, and answers at once: so that no one should exalt himself over another. The rabbis of the Mishnah had asked the same question of Adam and given the same answer, and from that meeting point this pilot follows the guide through all eight of its sections, a hundred of its quotations in the company of a hundred others. Some stand close: Saʿdī on the limbs of one body, a hadith and the Sermon on the Mount on what to wish for a brother, the Buddha on speech that divides, Cyprian on the rays of one sun. Others push back, or add what is missing. Augustine sorts humankind into two cities; Madison finds safety in a multiplicity of sects; Mill asks what is owed to the one person who disagrees; Kant fears that a world without separate states would end in despotism; Gandhi keeps his own house and opens its windows. The Bahá’í passages are not softened by the company, and the other voices are not made to agree with them. Each is placed beside the reading it answers, with a note saying why.
questions: What do the images of dust, tree, body and sea each claim about human oneness? Read Saʿdī, Paul and Marcus Aurelius beside them, and then Augustine’s two cities and Isaiah’s wolf and lamb. Where does each draw the boundary of “we”?

The readings hope for one common Faith, one city and a world without separate boundaries. Set beside them Qur’an 5:48, Gandhi, Hugo, Kant and Micah’s vine and fig tree. What distinguishes the unity the readings intend from uniformity, and from empire?

The golden rule appears here in five forms: the reading’s, the hadith’s, the Gospel’s, that of Confucius and Shaw’s reversal. What does each assume about the other person? Read Thoreau and Dostoevsky’s doctor beside the readings on kindness. What makes care for another welcome?

Several readings ask a community for one mind: “harmony of thought and absolute unity”, “a uniform body of opinion”, steadfastness in one Covenant. How do Aristotle, Milton, Mill and Madison each value difference of opinion? Which of their concerns do the readings already answer, and which remain open?

A common language, schools open to all, places of worship and mutual aid give unity practical forms. Compare Zamenhof, Babel and Goethe on language, and Garrison and Burke on country and kind. Which loyalties does a wider unity build on, and which must it replace?

The prayers at the end ask that hearts become as one heart and that this world reflect the Kingdom. What do the last hymn of the Rig Veda, the prayer of Jesus and the Lord’s Prayer share with them, and whom does each include?

findings.title: A proportional cut is the whole guide in small.
findings.text: Each of the eight sections keeps its share: 12, 16, 10, 17, 18, 12, 11 and 4 quotations. Conduct, consultation and the Covenant, institutions, peace and prayer, which the first version of this pilot lost by stopping at the first hundred quotations, are all here, and the outside voices had to answer them.

findings.title: In this guide, authorized translations were enough.
findings.text: Every section could fill its share from readings wholly in authorized translation, so the hundred quotations hold no provisional wording, and 117 of the guide’s 188 authorized paragraphs are kept where the first version kept 66. The balance of voices stays close to the whole guide’s: 23 quotations from Bahá’u’lláh, 39 from the tablets of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá and 38 from his talks.

findings.title: Few guides can be cut this way as they stand.
findings.text: The rule leans on two things this guide happens to have: named sections, which only 20 of the 186 long guides share, and authorized translations in plenty, which none of the other 19 has in every section. For the whole collection it would need sections marked in 166 guides, or another measure of spread, and it would usually leave provisional translations in the cut.

findings.title: Each section drew its own kind of company.
findings.text: The readings on a shared origin and on religion drew mostly parallels. The section on consultation, the Covenant and community life drew the most disagreement: Aristotle, Madison, Mill and Milton all prize difference of opinion where the readings ask for one mind. The four prayers of the last section were answered only by scripture.

findings.title: Reading against the content pulls toward the Bible.
findings.text: The readings on conduct, community and prayer speak of a shepherd and his sheep, of overlooking faults and of being of one heart, and their nearest and best-known parallels in English are biblical: 22 of the 100 come from the King James Bible, against 13 in the first version, and modern Europe and North America supply 37 more. Voices from Asia, Africa and the Islamic world number 28, and each needed a translation whose wording and rights had to be settled first.

findings.title: A parallel is rarely an equivalent.
findings.text: Most of the quotations placed “alongside” share an idea with their reading and differ in scope: a congregation, the believers, one nation, one household. The notes say so in each case; without them the page would suggest agreements that are not there.

outside.why: The rabbis ask the reading’s own question, why humankind began from a single person, and give its answer: so that no one can claim a greater ancestor than another. The Mishnah says it in a courtroom, while warning witnesses in a capital case.

“Created of one essence,” says Saʿdī of the children of Adam, where the reading says “from one same substance”, and both draw a duty from it. The reading asks for one soul; Saʿdī gives the test: whoever feels nothing at another’s pain does not deserve the name of human.

Kabīr’s hymn, kept in the Sikh scripture and using a Muslim name for God, joins the two opening readings: if the whole universe welled up from one Light, on what ground is one person ranked above another?

“Regard ye not one another as strangers,” says the reading. The Torah makes the same demand a law, for a people who remember being strangers themselves, and gives the measure: love the stranger as yourself.

The readings ground brotherhood in one God, one humankind, one globe and one sky. Speaking of a rival power in the Cold War, an American president keeps the globe and the air, adds children and mortality, and makes no appeal to religion.

The reading sets wolves, which live apart and fight, against the gentle animals that flock together. Hobbes says we are both: gods to one another inside a commonwealth, wolves between cities. A later reading hopes that all will be citizens of one city. Is the wolf in us a fault of character or a want of common institutions?

The reading divides the animals into those that prey and those that flock. Isaiah’s picture of peace does not sort them: the wolf itself comes to live with the lamb, and a child leads them. Is unity the fellowship of the gentle, or the change of the fierce?

“He has endowed them with equal susceptibilities,” says the reading. Shylock argues the same from the body, organ by organ, to men who have spat on him, and in the lines that follow he claims an equal right to revenge.

The reading asks us to love all humankind as leaves of one tree, and a later one to love all “with love of the heart”. A doctor in Dostoevsky’s novel admits the difficulty: love for humanity can grow as love for the person in the room shrinks. The elder who tells the story prescribes active love, practised on particular people.

The reading denies that humankind is two trees, one divine and one satanic. Augustine’s account of history does divide humankind, into two cities made by two loves, and it shaped Christian thought for a thousand years. He draws the line through what people love, not through birth, nation or creed. Does the reading deny that there are two loves, or that anyone may sort the leaves by them?

The reading is the first line of a talk that goes on to say that a tree or a bird may live alone, and a human being cannot. Donne, hearing a funeral bell from his sickbed, says the same of himself: no one is an island, and every death takes something from him.

The reading makes humanity a tree, its peoples the branches and each person a fruit or blossom. The emperor follows the image through: a branch may be cut off by another hand, but a person cuts himself off, by hatred, from the whole tree.

“One Lord, one faith, one baptism”: the letter gives the Christian form of the reading’s remedy, the union of all peoples in one common Faith, and its “one body, and one Spirit” stands close to a later reading’s “one soul and one body”.

The reading prescribes one common Faith as the remedy for the world’s ills. Gandhi, writing amid the quarrels of India’s religious communities, prescribes differently: not one religion but mutual respect among many. Are these rival answers, or answers to different questions?

The verse says God could have made humankind one community and did not. Each has its law and its way, all are to compete in good works, and God will settle their differences. How does plurality by design sit beside the reading’s one common Faith?

“The utterance of God is a lamp,” say two readings, and its light is the oneness of humankind. Rūmī had used lamp and light to explain how religions can differ and agree: the lamps are many, the light is one.

The reading hopes the earth’s inhabitants will become citizens of one city. Plutarch reports that the founder of Stoicism made this the single principle of his ideal state, and adds that Zeno wrote it as a dream.

The reading says the kernel of religion was lost and only the shell kept. The Quaker founder of Pennsylvania says the same of persons: the humble and merciful are everywhere of one religion, and only the liveries they wear make them strangers.

Paul’s sentence is the reading’s nearest ancestor: the labels of nation, rank and sex are named and set aside. He adds “in Christ Jesus”. The reading describes a gathering of people who have laid such prejudices down.

Among them, says the reading, no one says “I am a Persian” or “I am a Turk”. Du Bois describes a person who carries two names at once, feels them at war within him, and asks only to be allowed both. When does laying a name down unite, and when does it erase?

The reading names cooperation and reciprocity as humanity’s supreme need. Asked for one word to live by, Confucius chose the same one, and defined it by the rule a later reading gives as a condition of brotherhood.

Paul’s body, whose members cannot dismiss one another and suffer together, is the nearest scriptural parallel to the reading. He is writing to one congregation about its quarrels; the reading speaks of the entire human race.
The verse puts the reading’s argument in one sentence: all the wealth on earth could not have joined these hearts; God joined them.

The most famous call to unity of the modern age rests on the opposite premise. For Marx and Engels a shared material condition, not a spiritual power, will unite people across every border, and the unity is that of one class against another.

The reading takes its image from the last vision of the New Testament, where a holy city comes down and God’s tabernacle is “with men”. John sees a city and a people; the reading says what the city holds, the knowledge of earlier dispensations, and what it announces, the oneness of the children of men.
The prophet’s three questions follow the reading’s own order: one Father, one Creator, and therefore, why do we wrong one another?

The reading asks that the old hatred between religious systems give way to spiritual brotherhood. A rabbi speaking at a Christian seminary gives a reason: borrowing Donne’s island, he says the faiths are already bound together, and that the failure of one harms all.
Pascal, a believer, says how deep the old condition runs. Religious conviction does not merely fail to prevent harm; it can make harm complete and cheerful. What in a religion guards against this?

“Let no man exalt himself above another.” The rhyme a priest took as his text in the English rising of 1381 puts the same demand as a question about the first parents, whose one progeny, a later reading says, all mankind is.
The reading says the variety of humankind has a divine purpose. The verse names one: nations and tribes were made so that people may come to know one another, and honour lies in conduct, not descent.

A Daoist adds a warning to the reading’s praise of variety. To make the different alike, by lengthening the duck’s legs or shortening the crane’s, causes pain. What would it mean to unite people without doing that?

“Close your eyes to racial differences.” American law received the same image in 1896, when Justice Harlan wrote in dissent that the Constitution is colour-blind. Eighty-two years later a justice of the same court argued that the road to such a society runs first through seeing race. If the reading states the goal, does it also settle the means?

The play that gave America its best-known image of unity opened four years before ‘Abdu’l-Bahá spoke there, and its image is the reverse of his. In the crucible differences melt into one metal; in the garden each flower keeps its colour and lends charm to the rest.

Answering Zangwill three years after ‘Abdu’l-Bahá spoke of the garden, an American philosopher chose a kindred image: an orchestra in which each people keeps its own instrument and the music needs them all, discords included.

The words the reading quotes, “No difference canst thou see in the creation of the God of mercy”, are from this verse of the Qur’an. There they describe the heavens, made in harmony and without a rift; the reading says them of humankind, whom one Shepherd tends without favour.
Speaking to the United Nations, the emperor of Ethiopia made the reading’s link between the equality of races and the peace of the world, and stated it as a condition.

The most quoted sentence of the Atlanta address offered unity in work together with separation in social life. The reading asks for the first, “mutual advancement”, and other readings refuse the second. Can a hand be one if its fingers never touch?
India’s phrase for the reading’s “one great universal family”, vasudhaiva kuṭumbakam, comes from this verse, which treats the sorting of people into mine and theirs as a small mind’s arithmetic.

The reading lists those to be cared for: the ignorant, the sick, the child. The Gospel’s list is longer, and it adds a reason the reading leaves unsaid: what is done for the least of them is done for the one who speaks.

Thoreau speaks for the person on the receiving end. The readings would have the ignorant educated and the sick healed, as by a kind physician; he would run from anyone who arrived with that design. What separates the love the readings ask for from the goodness Thoreau fears?

The reading argues from creation to love: God must have loved all equally, or He would not have created them, and He would not protect what He did not love. A Jewish book written in Greek around the turn of the era takes the same two steps in the same order.

The Shepherd of the readings trains, educates and cures his flock. In Ezekiel God takes the work on himself, after shepherds who fed themselves and not the sheep: he will seek the lost, bind up the broken and strengthen the sick. The verse then judges the fat and the strong, where the reading’s Shepherd is kind to all.
The reading and the hadith are almost one sentence: to wish for a brother what one wishes for oneself. The reading says first who the brother is: “The children of men are all brothers.”

In the Sermon on the Mount the rule is about deeds and covers everyone, and Jesus calls it the sum of the law and the prophets. The reading states it of wishes, as one among many prerequisites of brotherhood.
Shaw’s joke carries a real objection. To wish for another what one wishes for oneself assumes that people want the same things. How does one learn what a brother wishes for himself?

In the reading, streams and drops gathered into a sea lose the distinctions they had. A father in the Upanishad teaches his son with the same waters: rivers that have reached the sea no longer know “I am this or that river”. He is speaking of all creatures and their source; the reading, of peoples and their customs.

The reading expects traditions, customs and distinctions to vanish like drops in the sea. Closing the first Parliament of Religions, a Hindu monk set a limit to merging: each should take in the spirit of the others and still grow by its own law. Which distinctions does unity dissolve, and which does it keep?

The reading asks people to concern themselves at all times with doing a kindly thing for one of their fellows. Marley’s ghost learned it too late: the common welfare had been his business all along, and his trade a drop in its ocean.
On the interconnection of all its parts, says the reading, depends the flourishing of every leaf of the world-tree. The emperor says the same of the swarm and the bee, in one sentence.

“Close your eyes to the deficiencies of other souls,” says the reading, and let your thoughts dwell on your own development. The Dhammapada gives the same counsel in almost the same form; the Gospel gives it with a mote and a beam.

The verse that commands love of neighbour first commands something the reading leaves out: to rebuke him openly, so that hatred is not kept in the heart. The reading asks us to close our eyes to others’ faults. When is silence about a fault kindness, and when is it a grudge?

“How good it is if the friends be as close as sheaves of light.” The reading opens on the cadence of the best-known verse on unity in the Hebrew Bible, which praises the same thing: people dwelling together as one.

The friends are to “stand together side by side in a firm unbroken line” and become as one soul. Gibran, speaking of marriage, uses the same verb and adds a measure: together, yet not too near, like the pillars of a temple. Does his counsel to two people hold for a community?

The reading would win the materially minded “by the radiance of your kindness”. The fable makes the same wager with the same image: the wind’s force only tightens the traveller’s cloak, and the sun’s warmth takes it off.

The reading asks the friends to overlook one another’s faults, as a token of love. Pope’s line, written about how critics should treat authors, became the proverb for it: fault is human, and forgiving it is the divine part.

The reading’s images for an assembly, rays of one sun, drops of one river, trees of one orchard, are those a bishop of Carthage used in 251 to plead against schism: rays, branches and streams live only from their one source. Both writers are guarding the unity of a community of faith.

The reading makes “harmony of thought and absolute unity” the condition of an assembly’s life. Aristotle, criticising Plato, warns of a point at which unity defeats itself, “like harmony passing into unison”. What keeps the harmony the reading asks for from becoming unison?

“If they cannot unite around one point how will they be able to bring about the unity of mankind?” Lincoln, quoting the Gospel, put the same law to a nation half slave and half free: what is divided against itself cannot stand.

The reading holds that only the Covenant, kept according to its explicit Text, can preserve unity. The Qur’an gives a community the same instruction in an image of its own: hold fast, all together, to God’s cable, and do not separate. It recalls what the readings hope for, enemies whose hearts were joined.

The reading dreads a new sect each day as the ruin of a Faith. Madison, designing a republic, welcomed the same multiplicity as a safeguard: where sects and interests are many, none can oppress the rest. One speaks of keeping a religion whole, the other of keeping a state free. Can both be right?
The reading warns against making the instrument of union an occasion for discord. A clergyman’s dry sentence reports the warning unheeded: religion enough to hate by, and not enough to love by.

“Backbiting is divisive,” says the reading, and it asks the friends to speak of one another only to praise. The Buddha’s account of right speech has the same two halves: carrying no tales that break people apart, and saying what reconciles the divided and cements the united.

The reading calls speaking ill of the absent the leading cause of withdrawal among friends. The Qur’an forbids it with an image no hearer forgets, the eating of a dead brother’s flesh, and begins further back than the reading does, with suspicion and spying.

The reading asks the friends to “stand for a uniform body of opinion” and put aside their conflicting views. Milton, defending the freedom to print in a nation full of sects, held that many opinions are a sign of learning in progress, and that forbearance and charity could still join them in one brotherly search after truth. Is his search a rival to the reading’s unity, or a road to it?

The reading expects the friends’ own concord to be the cause of spreading the oneness of humanity. In the Gospel the disciples are given the same mark: everyone will know them by their love for one another.

Paul asks a quarrelling church for what the reading announces: that all “speak the same thing”, with one mind, one judgment and no divisions. He was writing to believers who had begun to name themselves after their teachers.

The reading looks to a day when thoughts and beliefs meet at a single point and disputes disappear. Mill supposes the day almost come, all of humankind but one of a single opinion, and asks what is owed to that one. How is the unity of thought the reading describes reached, and what becomes in it of the person not yet persuaded?

The reading turns everyone toward a single centre, and an earlier one says what the alternative is: a new sect each day and utter division. Yeats, writing after the Great War, gave that fear its best-known words.

One reading foresees the world as one household, and another asks the friends to be father and mother to the orphan and sons and daughters to the old. The Confucian picture of the age of Grand Union is close to both: a common spirit rules all under the sky, and people care for more than their own parents and children. The classic places that age in the past; the readings place it ahead.

One reading sees East and West as one household, and another has them hold each other close like two lovers. Kipling’s famous line says they will never meet, and his quatrain then allows one exception: there is neither East nor West when two strong men stand face to face.

The reading calls kindly fellowship with all peoples the very foundation of God’s law. The verse permits kindness and justice toward people of another religion and marks a limit the reading does not: it speaks of those who have not made war on the believers or driven them from their homes.

“Whoso seeketh shelter under this roof will certainly come forth from other dwellings.” The best-known such leaving in scripture is Ruth’s, who gives up her own people and their gods to lodge where Naomi lodges.

The reading expects those who shelter under the roof of oneness to come out of their other dwellings. Gandhi keeps his house and opens it: every culture may blow through, and none shall blow him off his feet. Must one leave a house to live under a wider roof?

The reading says the law of the struggle for existence is abrogated. The naturalist who put that struggle at the centre of his theory expected something of the kind among human beings: as communities grow, reason tells each person to extend sympathy to the whole nation, and after that only “an artificial barrier” stands between him and all nations and races.

Tennyson gives the doubt its best-known words. His mourner had trusted that love is creation’s final law, while nature, “red in tooth and claw”, cried out against that creed. The reading says the struggle is abrogated through the breaths of the Holy Spirit; the poem leaves the question open.

In 1887 the inventor of Esperanto argued as the reading does: with one international language there would be only two to learn, and the first cause of dislike between peoples, not being understood, would go.

Scripture’s own story of one people with one language ends with God confounding their speech and scattering them, because nothing would be beyond their reach. The readings look to a common language as a means of unity. What separates the unity they hope for from the unity of Babel?

The reading tells of peoples who hoped to rise by speaking their own tongue alone and purging it of everything foreign. Goethe gives a reason of another kind against them: a language is understood only by those who know a second one.

The reading opens a school for Bahá’í children to the children of others. Confucius gives the principle its shortest form; the reading applies it across a line he did not have in view, that of religion.

The reading lets the school teach an outline of the principles underlying all religions. An emperor of India had urged as much on grown subjects more than two thousand years earlier, in an edict cut into rock: listen to the doctrines of others, and respect them.

“Let not man glory in this that he loveth his country, let him rather glory in this that he loveth his kind.” An American abolitionist had made nearly the same thought the motto of his newspaper in 1831.

The reading sets love of one’s kind above love of country. Burke orders the two differently: love of the small group one belongs to is the first link in a chain that leads on to love of country and of mankind. Can the wider loyalty be learned without the nearer one?

The reading’s phrase “mutual aid” is the title a Russian geographer gave his book of 1902. He argued the case from natural history, against those who read Darwin as a licence for unlimited competition: the animals that combine are the ones that thrive.
Places of worship, says the reading, are founded so that humanity may find a place of meeting. Isaiah has God say it of the Temple in Jerusalem, speaking of the foreigners who join themselves to him.

“The real temple is the very Word of God,” says the reading, turning from buildings to what gathers people. The Andalusian mystic makes a turn of his own in a love poem, where his heart has become cloister, temple, Kaaba and Torah at once. The reading finds the centre in a Word to which all must turn; the poet, in a heart that can take every form.
“This span of earth is but one homeland.” The oldest recorded form of that claim is a philosopher’s reply to a question about his home town.

The reading’s shelter is a tabernacle wide enough for all peoples. The Great Law of the Haudenosaunee plants a tree for the same purpose: its roots run to the four directions, so that any nation willing to keep the peace may follow one to its shade.

Peace among nations, says the reading, must begin among individuals. The Confucian classic lays out the same order of steps: the person cultivated, then the family, the state, and at last a whole kingdom at peace.

The founders of UNESCO began where the reading does, inside persons: wars start in the minds of men, and peace must be defended there. Their means is knowledge of each other’s ways and lives; the reading’s is love created through the power of the Word of God.

The reading foretells that the dignity and equality of every servant of God will be acknowledged. The Declaration, written after a world war for peoples of every belief, makes the acknowledgement in the reading’s own words, dignity, equality and brotherhood, and names no ground but reason and conscience.
Orwell’s pigs keep the commandment and add a clause. The line warns every community that proclaims equality: the words can stay on the wall after the practice has gone.

The reading’s green pastures and wellspring are those of the best-known psalm. There one person speaks of “my shepherd”; the reading makes the flock all the children of men, and calls that the precept of the oneness of mankind.

The reading foresees the end of nations with separate and restricted boundaries. Hugo, opening a peace congress in Paris in 1849, foresaw the nations of Europe blended into a higher unity “without losing your distinctive qualities and your glorious individuality”. Does the reading’s oneness need the boundaries gone, or only their power to divide?

Kant wanted perpetual peace as much as the reading does, and feared its shortcut. A world fused into one state by a power grown over the rest would, he thought, end in soulless despotism, so he proposed a federation of states that stay separate. The reading says oneness will supplant “the banner of conquest”. What would keep a world without separate nations from becoming Kant’s universal monarchy?

The reading foresees countries so closely connected that humanity becomes one family. Writing from a jail cell to clergymen who had called him an outsider, King described the connection as already a fact and drew its consequence: what affects one directly affects all indirectly.

The reading hopes for countries intimately connected and peoples commingled. The Daoist classic imagines the opposite as the happy state: a small country whose people can hear their neighbours’ fowls and dogs and grow old without ever visiting them. What does each picture fear?

The prayer asks that the warfare of thousands of years may end and all find tranquillity beneath one tabernacle. The prophet shares the hope, swords beaten into ploughshares, and ends it differently: each man under his own vine, and each people walking in the name of its own god. Can the peace of the first verse be had together with the plurality of the last?

The reading is the prayer of one who has made an offering so that all on earth may be united. In the Gospel, on the night before his death, Jesus prays “that they all may be one”, and the words became the charter of every movement for Christian unity. Their scope is those who will believe; the reading names all that dwell on earth.

The prayer gives thanks that hearts have become as a single heart. The last hymn of the Rig Veda, some three thousand years older, asks for the same: one resolve, minds of one accord, a common assembly and a common purpose.

“Pray for this!” The reading asks prayer that this world may become the reflection of the eternal Kingdom. The most repeated prayer of Christianity asks it in a line: thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven.

leftOut.saying: “If there is to be peace in the world, there must be peace in the nations … there must be peace in the heart.”
leftOut.reason: Wanted beside the reading on peace among individuals, and left out: it is not in Legge’s translation of the Tao Te Ching, and Wikiquote’s page for Laozi does not list it. The Great Learning, which does say something close, stands there instead.

leftOut.saying: “Lord, make me an instrument of your peace.”
leftOut.attributed: Known as the Prayer of Saint Francis.
leftOut.reason: Considered for the last section and left out. Wikipedia records that the prayer is absent from the writings of Francis and has not been traced further back than a French magazine of December 1912, so it could enter only as an anonymous prayer of that year, and no English wording with a named translator was settled.

leftOut.saying: “If you want to go fast, go alone; if you want to go far, go together.”
leftOut.reason: No source for it as the proverb of any people was established in this pilot, so it was left out.

leftOut.saying: “Be the change you wish to see in the world.”
leftOut.reason: Left out unverified: no place in his writings was found for it. Two passages from Young India, with their dates, are used instead.

leftOut.saying: “Man did not weave the web of life; he is merely a strand in it.”
leftOut.reason: Left out: the attribution is doubtful and no primary text was reached. The Great Law of Peace stands as the voice from Indigenous North America.

leftOut.saying: The songs “Imagine”, “One Love” and “We Are the World”.
leftOut.attributed: John Lennon; Bob Marley; Michael Jackson and Lionel Richie.
leftOut.reason: Among the best-known statements of the theme, and omitted: song lyrics are licensed more strictly than other texts, and no line of a lyric is quoted in this pilot.
